## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
Sekhiya 41 of the Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga (entitled *Anāhaṭa*, translated as "Opening the mouth") is an etiquette training rule in the Theravāda Vinaya Piṭaka regulating monastic decorum during meals, specifically proscribing the opening of the mouth before food has been brought to it [SuttaCentral]. An English translation of the text and its case narrative is provided by Bhikkhu Brahmali [SuttaCentral]. No discussions of this rule appear in the provided secondary literature.
According to SuttaCentral, this training rule has comprehensive parallels across early Buddhist monastic traditions. It corresponds to rule 41 of the Theravāda *Bhikkhupātimokkha*, the *Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga*, and the *Parivāra*, as well as bhikkhu and bhikkhunī rules preserved in Sanskrit, Tibetan, and Chinese across the Dharmaguptaka, Kāśyapīya, Mahāsāṅghika, Mahīśāsaka, Mūlasarvāstivāda, and Sarvāstivāda traditions, in addition to the *Upāliparipṛcchā* [SuttaCentral]. Internally within the Pali canon, DharmaNexus detects 75 matching text-reuse passages across 27 Vinaya texts [DharmaNexus]. The strongest alignments are with other Sekhiya rules—most prominently Sekhiya 43 (§0.1–1.2), Sekhiya 42 (§1.3.1–1.9), Sekhiya 61, and Sekhiya 17—due to the heavily formulaic opening setting narratives and shared exemption clauses common to the mealtime training rules [DharmaNexus].
*No discussion of this text was found in the reference-literature corpus; the overview relies on SuttaCentral and DharmaNexus data.*
